summary:
Eastern Cape stands under the national framework of South Africa. The province's trans-relevant law is the national layer: the constitutional prohibition on unfair discrimination, the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act and its Equality Court, the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024, and legal gender recognition under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003.

Transgender prisoners held in Eastern Cape correctional centres, among them St Albans, Mthatha and East London, are governed by the national placement standard rather than any provincial rule. Under the regulations to the Correctional Services Act on the accommodation of vulnerable inmates, and the Department of Correctional Services' standard operating procedures, inmates are to be housed in cells appropriate to their gender identity where that is feasible and safe, and transgender inmates are to be held in single cells. No Eastern Cape-specific transgender placement case is on record, so the province's custody practice is read entirely from the national instruments.

Rural districts under customary jurisdiction carry a risk that does not apply in the metropolitan centres. A bill before the national parliament in 2012 would have created a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustan areas, with no opt-out from customary jurisdiction. Human Rights Watch reported at the time that rural LGBT people already faced discrimination, violence and poor cooperation from police, and that chiefs' courts punished lesbians in rural areas.

Gender-affirming care in the province runs through the public hospital system and is documented as slow. In December 2024 LGBT activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over year-long delays in transgender healthcare. A trans visitor who depends on the public system in the Eastern Cape should plan for waiting times rather than immediate access.
tangentialFactors:
Eastern Cape police arrested four suspects in May 2025 over the killings of two women in Gqeberha, whose bodies were found at separate locations the previous week. The deaths prompted public outrage and renewed calls to confront gender-based violence in the province. The incident is not recorded as trans-specific, and the sources supply no provincial homicide rate against which to read it.

Violence data for the province is not disaggregated by gender identity, so no Eastern Cape-specific rate of violence against transgender people can be stated. The national protection machinery, including the 2024 hate-crimes legislation and the rapid response arrangements for unsolved cases, applies here without a provincial counterpart.

outOfScopeNotes:
The parliamentary fate of the customary-courts bill reported by Human Rights Watch in 2012 is not recorded in the sources, so whether customary jurisdiction currently operates as that bill proposed is unresolved.

No Eastern Cape-specific case on transgender prisoner placement is on record. The operative rule is the national standard, and its application in the province's correctional centres has not been tested in the sources.

No provincial data disaggregating violence by gender identity is available. The May 2025 Gqeberha killings are not recorded as trans-specific, and no Eastern Cape homicide rate appears in the sources for comparison.

No Eastern Cape-specific provision on identity documents, facilities access or entry appears in the sources; those matters are governed by the national framework.
